subtopic: Oscillations: mean position, displacement and amplitude
learning_objective: Students will be able to locate the mean position of an oscillating body, measure displacement from it, find the amplitude as half the distance between the extreme positions, and tell periodic, oscillatory and simple harmonic motion apart.
statement: In an oscillation, displacement is measured from the mean (equilibrium) position, and the amplitude is the maximum displacement: the distance from the mean position to either extreme, which is half the extreme-to-extreme distance.
simple: An oscillating body goes back and forth around the point where it would rest, called the mean position. How far it is from that point right now is its displacement. The farthest it ever gets from that point is the amplitude. So the amplitude is only half the gap between the two ends.
formal: Periodic motion repeats after equal intervals of time. Oscillatory motion is periodic to-and-fro motion about a mean position, where the net force on the body is zero. Simple harmonic motion is the special oscillation in which the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position, F = -kx. Displacement x is measured from the mean position and varies between +A and -A. The extreme positions are at x = ±A, so they are 2A apart.

equations.meaning: Displacement from the mean position at time t in SHM
Distance between the two extreme positions is twice the amplitude
equations.assumptions: symmetric oscillation about the mean position, no damping

equations.meaning: Restoring force in SHM is proportional to displacement and points towards the mean position
equations.assumptions: ideal SHM; small displacements for a pendulum

analogy: A park swing: the lowest point, where it would hang at rest, is the mean position. The amplitude is how far the seat gets from that lowest point on one side, not the full distance from the front end to the back end.
steps: Locate the mean position: where the body would rest with zero net force, midway between the extremes
Measure displacement from the mean position, with a sign showing the side
Mark the extremes, where the displacement is largest: x = +A and x = -A
Take the amplitude as half the distance between the two extremes
Call the motion SHM only if the restoring force is proportional to -x
worked_example: A block oscillates between extremes 0.20 m apart. A = 0.20 m / 2 = 0.10 m. When it is 0.04 m from one extreme, its displacement from the mean is 0.10 - 0.04 = 0.06 m, on that extreme's side. If it starts at that extreme at t = 0, x = 0.10 cos(ωt) m, so φ = 0.
alternatives: Picture a number line with zero at the mean position: the body runs between -A and +A. It travels 2A from one end to the other, but its amplitude is just A.
Every SHM is periodic, but not every periodic motion is SHM: Earth's orbit and a bouncing ball repeat, yet neither has a restoring force F = -kx about a mean position.

subtopic: Velocity and acceleration of a particle in SHM
learning_objective: Students will be able to state and explain where the speed and the acceleration of an ideal simple harmonic oscillator are maximum and zero, give the direction of the acceleration, and calculate v and a at any displacement.
statement: In ideal SHM the speed is greatest at the mean position and zero at the extremes, while the acceleration is zero at the mean, greatest at the extremes, and always directed toward the mean.
simple: Think of a block on a spring. In the middle the spring is relaxed, so nothing pushes the block and it is moving fastest. At the ends it stops for an instant, but the spring is stretched most, so the pull back is strongest there.
formal: For x = A cos(ωt + φ), the velocity is v = −Aω sin(ωt + φ) = ±ω√(A² − x²) and the acceleration is a = −ω²x. Speed is therefore maximum (Aω) at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A. Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite to it: zero at the mean and of maximum magnitude ω²A at the extremes. Velocity and acceleration are out of phase by π/2, so one is largest when the other is zero.

equations.meaning: velocity at time t for x = A cos(ωt + φ)
speed at displacement x; maximum Aω at x = 0, zero at x = ±A
acceleration is proportional to displacement and points toward the mean; zero at x = 0, magnitude ω²A at x = ±A
kinetic energy is greatest at the mean position and zero at the extremes

analogy: A child on a jhoola: she whooshes fastest through the bottom, where nothing tugs her forward or back, and pauses at the highest points, where the pull back down toward the bottom is strongest.
steps: Locate the oscillator: find its displacement x from the mean position.
Acceleration follows displacement: a = −ω²x, so it is zero at x = 0, largest at x = ±A, and always points toward the mean.
Speed follows the opposite pattern: v = ω√(A² − x²), so it is largest at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A.
Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration: at the extremes the body is only turning around.
Check with energy: at the mean all energy is kinetic; at the extremes all is potential.
worked_example: A block oscillates with A = 0.1 m and ω = 10 rad/s. At the mean: v = Aω = 1 m/s, a = 0. At an extreme: v = 0, |a| = ω²A = 100 × 0.1 = 10 m/s², toward the mean. At x = 0.06 m: v = 10√(0.01 − 0.0036) = 10 × 0.08 = 0.8 m/s and a = −100 × 0.06 = −6 m/s².
alternatives: Use force: the spring force F = −kx is zero at the mean and largest at the extremes, so by F = ma the acceleration follows the same pattern. The block speeds up while moving toward the mean and slows down after passing it, so its speed peaks exactly at the mean.

Use the circle: SHM is the shadow of uniform circular motion. At the centre of the shadow's path the point on the circle moves parallel to the line, so the shadow moves fastest; at the ends it moves perpendicular, so the shadow stops while the centripetal pull is fully along the line.

subtopic: Time period, frequency and angular frequency
learning_objective: Students will be able to convert between T, f and ω, calculate the period of a spring–mass system and a simple pendulum, and explain why the period does not depend on amplitude in ideal SHM.
statement: In SHM the period T = 2π/ω is fixed by the system (m and k, or L and g), not by how far it is pulled.
simple: The time period is the time for one full back-and-forth. Frequency is how many back-and-forths happen in one second. A heavier block on a spring swings slower, but a heavier pendulum bob does not. Pulling further does not change the time.
formal: For SHM x = A cos(ωt + φ), the motion repeats when ωt advances by 2π, so T = 2π/ω and f = 1/T = ω/2π. Angular frequency ω (rad/s) is therefore 2π times f (Hz). For a spring–mass system ω = √(k/m), giving T = 2π√(m/k). For a simple pendulum at small angles ω = √(g/L), giving T = 2π√(L/g), independent of bob mass. Amplitude A does not appear in ω, so the period is amplitude-independent.

equations.meaning: one full cycle is 2π radians of phase
number of oscillations per second
angular frequency is 2π times ordinary frequency
period of a spring–mass oscillator
period of a simple pendulum
equations.assumptions: small angles, point bob, light inextensible string

analogy: A merry-go-round turning at a fixed rate: a child on the outer edge covers a bigger circle but moves faster, so every child takes the same time per round.
steps: Identify the system: spring–mass or simple pendulum
Find ω from the system: √(k/m) or √(g/L)
Get T = 2π/ω and f = 1/T, never T = 1/ω
Check what changed: amplitude does not affect T; spring mass does; pendulum bob mass does not
worked_example: A 0.25 kg block on a spring with k = 25π² N/m: ω = √(25π²/0.25) = 10π rad/s, so T = 2π/10π = 0.2 s and f = 5 Hz, whether the amplitude is 2 cm or 4 cm.
alternatives: Think in terms of phase: the block finishes a cycle when ωt grows by 2π radians, so T is 2π/ω seconds; f counts cycles, ω counts radians.
A bigger amplitude means a bigger restoring force at the ends, so the block moves faster; the extra speed exactly cancels the extra distance.

subtopic: Restoring force and the defining condition a = −ω²x
learning_objective: Students will be able to state that the restoring force in SHM is proportional to displacement and always directed toward the mean position, and use a = −ω²x with ω² = k/m to find acceleration at any displacement.
statement: In SHM the restoring force F = −kx grows with displacement and always points toward the mean position, so a = −ω²x with ω² = k/m.
simple: Pull a block on a spring and let go. The spring always pulls it back toward the middle. The farther you pull, the harder it pulls back. At the middle, the pull is zero.
formal: A particle performs SHM when the net force on it is a restoring force proportional to its displacement from the mean position and opposite in direction: F = −kx. By Newton's second law, ma = −kx, so a = −(k/m)x = −ω²x, where ω = √(k/m) is the angular frequency. The condition a ∝ −x defines SHM. The acceleration is zero at the mean and has maximum magnitude ω²A at the extremes, whatever the direction of velocity.

equations.meaning: Restoring force is proportional to displacement and opposite to it
Defining condition of SHM: acceleration proportional to displacement, directed toward the mean
Angular frequency is fixed by the stiffness and the mass

analogy: A ball in a round bowl: wherever you push it, the slope always tips it back toward the bottom, and the farther up the side, the steeper the slope and the stronger the tip back.
steps: Locate the mean position and measure the displacement x from it
The restoring force is F = −kx: its size is k|x| and its direction is toward the mean
Ignore which way the body is moving; only the displacement sets the force
Divide by mass: a = −(k/m)x = −ω²x
Check: zero at the mean, largest (ω²A) at the extremes
worked_example: m = 0.25 kg, k = 100 N/m, block at x = +0.03 m. F = −kx = −100 × 0.03 = −3 N (toward mean). ω² = k/m = 400 s⁻², so ω = 20 rad/s and a = −ω²x = −400 × 0.03 = −12 m/s², i.e. 12 m/s² toward the mean.
alternatives: Think of the spring as always trying to undo the stretch: it pulls in when stretched and pushes out when compressed, so the force always points back to the natural length, and a bigger stretch means a bigger correction.
On an a–x graph, SHM is a straight line through the origin with negative slope −ω²; any other shape (constant a, positive slope, curve) is not SHM.

learning_objective: Students will be able to find the kinetic, potential and total energy of a body in SHM at any displacement, and explain why the total stays constant and grows as the square of the amplitude.
statement: In ideal SHM, kinetic and potential energy keep trading places, but their sum stays fixed at ½kA².
simple: A block on a spring keeps swapping two kinds of energy. In the middle it moves fastest, so it has the most kinetic energy and the spring stores none. At the ends it stops for an instant and the stretched spring stores all the energy. The total never changes if nothing rubs.
formal: For x = A cos(ωt + φ), the kinetic energy is KE = ½mω²(A² − x²) and the potential energy is PE = ½kx² = ½mω²x², with k = mω². Their sum is E = ½kA² = ½mω²A², independent of x and t, so total mechanical energy is conserved in undamped SHM. KE is maximum (equal to E) at the mean position and zero at the extremes; PE does the opposite. Because E depends on A², doubling the amplitude makes the energy four times larger.

equations.meaning: Total mechanical energy, the same at every position
Kinetic energy at displacement x; maximum at the mean, zero at the extremes
Potential energy at displacement x; zero at the mean, maximum at the extremes
equations.assumptions: PE taken as zero at the mean position; k = mω²

equations.meaning: The two energies always add to the same total

analogy: Like money moving between your wallet and your pocket while you walk: one fills as the other empties, but the total you carry stays the same.
steps: Find the total energy from the amplitude: E = ½kA².
Find the potential energy at the given position: PE = ½kx².
Get the kinetic energy as what is left: KE = E − PE.
Check the ends: at x = 0 all energy is KE; at x = ±A all of it is PE.
If the amplitude changes, scale the energy by the square of the factor.
alternatives: Graph view: plot PE = ½kx² as a U-shaped curve and E as a flat line at ½kA². At any x, the gap between the line and the curve is the KE.

Work view: the spring does positive work on the block while it moves toward the mean and negative work while it moves away, so energy only shuttles between spring and block; no outside force adds or removes any.

statement: Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium, away entering a rarer one; TIR needs denser-to-rarer travel beyond the critical angle.
analogy: A cycle rolling slantwise onto sand turns one way; back onto road, the other way.
steps: Compare n on both sides
Denser side: ray nearer the normal
Denser to rarer? sin C = n2/n1
TIR only if incidence angle exceeds C
worked_example: Glass to air, n = 1.5: sin C = 1/1.5, C ≈ 41.8°. At 45° inside: TIR. At 30°: exits at 48.6°.
subtopic: Refraction at a plane surface and total internal reflection
learning_objective: Predict whether a ray bends toward or away from the normal, use n = c/v and Snell's law, and decide when total internal reflection can occur.
simple: Light slows down in glass or water and speeds up again in air. Slowing down makes it bend toward the normal; speeding up makes it bend away. If light inside glass or water meets the surface at too steep an angle, it cannot get out and reflects back completely: total internal reflection.
formal: The refractive index of a medium is n = c/v, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium. At a boundary, Snell's law n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r fixes the refracted direction. Frequency is set by the source and stays the same, so the wavelength becomes λ_vacuum/n. For travel from a denser to a rarer medium, the critical angle C obeys sin C = n₂/n₁; for incidence beyond C there is no refracted ray and all the light is reflected.

equations.meaning: Refractive index compares the speed of light in vacuum with its speed in the medium.

vars.v: speed of light in the medium (m/s)

equations.expr: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r
equations.meaning: Snell's law links the angles on the two sides of a boundary.

vars.n₁: refractive index of first medium (no unit)
vars.n₂: refractive index of second medium (no unit)
vars.i: angle of incidence from the normal (degree)
vars.r: angle of refraction from the normal (degree)

equations.assumptions: Angles measured from the normal; plane boundary.

equations.meaning: Wavelength shrinks by the factor n while frequency stays fixed.
equations.assumptions: Frequency is set by the source and does not change at a boundary.

equations.expr: sin C = n₂ / n₁ (= 1/n into air)
equations.meaning: Critical angle beyond which total internal reflection occurs.

vars.n₁: refractive index of denser medium (no unit)
vars.n₂: refractive index of rarer medium (no unit)

equations.assumptions: Only defined for n₁ > n₂, light travelling denser to rarer; TIR when i > C.

alternatives: Wavefront view: one edge of a slanting wavefront reaches the slower medium first and lags behind, so the whole wavefront swings round; entering a faster medium swings it the other way.
Marching band view: a row of marchers stepping slantwise from road onto mud slows at one end first and wheels toward the normal; stepping back onto road wheels it away.

statement: Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium and away from it entering a rarer one.
wrong_idea: Whenever light goes into something new, it bends toward the normal.
why_it_feels_right: Most diagrams show air into glass or water, where it really does bend toward the normal.
why_wrong: The direction matters: going into a rarer medium like air, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
sim_moment: Refraction visual: drag the ray inside the glass and let it leave into air; it swings away from the normal. Drag it in from air and it swings toward.

statement: TIR needs denser-to-rarer travel and an incidence angle above the critical angle.
wrong_idea: If the angle is big enough, light totally reflects at any surface, from either side.
why_it_feels_right: Glass and water look shiny from both sides, and 'more than critical' is easy to remember alone.
why_wrong: From air into glass a refracted ray always exists; only light already in the denser medium can be trapped.
sim_moment: Refraction visual: inside the glass, drag the ray past the critical angle and watch TIR trap it. Now aim it in from the air side at 80°; it always enters.

statement: A convex lens forms a full real image where rays meet, screen or not.
analogy: Like a crowd using half the gates: everyone still gets out, slower.
steps: Use 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, u negative.
Each object point lights the whole lens, so covering part only dims the image.
Rays meet at v anyway; a screen just scatters them.
subtopic: Thin lenses: lens formula and image formation
learning_objective: Use 1/v − 1/u = 1/f and m = v/u to locate the image formed by a convex lens, and explain why covering part of the lens or removing the screen does not remove a real image.
simple: A convex lens bends light from every point of an object so the rays meet again on the other side. Where they meet, a real image forms, whether or not a screen is there. Every part of the lens helps make every part of the image, so covering half of it only makes the image dimmer.
formal: In the Cartesian sign convention, distances are measured from the optical centre and are positive in the direction of incident light, so a real object has negative u and a convex lens has positive f. The lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f gives the image distance and m = v/u the magnification. Positive v means a real, inverted image on the far side; negative v means a virtual, upright one. Blocking part of the aperture reduces brightness, not the extent of the image.

equations.meaning: Lens formula linking object distance, image distance and focal length.

vars.v: image distance from optical centre (cm or m)
vars.u: object distance from optical centre (cm or m)
vars.f: focal length, positive for convex (cm or m)

equations.assumptions: Thin lens, paraxial rays, Cartesian sign convention; check against the board textbook.

equations.meaning: Magnification: image size relative to object size; negative means inverted.
equations.assumptions: Same sign convention as the lens formula; heights above the axis positive.

alternatives: Ray-diagram view: draw two principal rays from the top of the object, one parallel to the axis and one through the optical centre; they cross at the image whether or not any surface is there.
Funnel view: the lens collects light from each object point over its whole face and pours it into one image point; a smaller opening pours less light, but into the same point.

statement: Covering part of a lens still gives the full image, only dimmer.
wrong_idea: If I cover the top half of the lens, the top half of the image disappears.
why_it_feels_right: Covering half a window hides half the view, so covering a lens seems to hide half the picture.
why_wrong: Each object point sends rays to the whole lens, so the open half still brings light from every point to the image.
sim_moment: Lens-bench visual: turn on 'cover half the lens' and watch the principal rays from the object still meet at the image; the whole image stays, only fainter.

statement: A real image forms where rays converge; a screen only scatters its light so it can be seen from many angles.
wrong_idea: If there's no screen, there's no real image. It just doesn't form.
why_it_feels_right: In the lab we only ever notice the real image when it lands on the screen.
why_wrong: Rays meet at the image point with or without a screen; an eye or camera beyond it sees the image in air.
sim_moment: Lens-bench visual: remove the screen and watch the principal rays still cross at the image point, then spread out beyond it.
